title: Lloyd's moves to redefine war as grey-zone conflict exposes gaps in century-old exclusions
key_claim: The Lloyd's Market Association is reviewing the post-1945 Five Powers war exclusion; draft wordings shared with the Financial Times list cyberattacks, drone incursions and undersea sabotage as scenarios that would not on their own trigger the exclusion, the LMA is weighing an independent panel to rule on whether a conflict counts as war, and it has not decided whether to publish the clause. Merck's NotPetya war-exclusion dispute settled in 2024 for a reported $1.4 billion; London market net underwriting results fell 14% to £4.8 billion in 2024.
frame_summary: The article argues that the London market is trying to write down where the line between peacetime hostility and war sits at the moment that line is hardest to draw, and that the effort runs against a softening market cycle and an open question of whether a London panel's ruling would bind a US court.
verbatim_quote: The drafts list scenarios that would not, on their own, trigger the exclusion - including cyberattacks, drone incursions and undersea sabotage.
verbatim_list: The Lloyd's Market Association is reviewing the Five Powers exclusion - a marine clause dating to the years after 1945 that cancels cover if war breaks out between the US, UK, France, China or Russia - because the binary it assumes is no longer the binary the world is operating in.
The case settled confidentially in 2024 for a reported $1.4 billion.
The LMA is weighing an independent panel to rule on whether a conflict counts as war for insurance purposes.

The LMA has not decided whether to publish the clause - insurers could adopt it or not. Past LMA wordings, including its sanctions clause, have shaped market practice well beyond Lloyd's, suggesting adoption could be broad if the wording achieves consensus.

London market net underwriting results fell 14% to £4.8 billion in 2024, down from £5.5 billion in 2023, and property rates dropped roughly 9% through the first half of 2025, according to Oxbow Partners data.

title: Kremlin's factory threat puts UK manufacturers' risk cover back in the spotlight
key_claim: A Kremlin-linked adviser told the BBC that British factories supplying drones and missile parts to Ukraine could face 'semi-military' action from 'unknown sources'; a state-linked cyber intrusion took a UK power generation facility offline for four days in July; Pool Re's cover typically applies to certified acts of terrorism rather than state-linked sabotage or acts of war; UK insurers paid close to £200 million in cyber claims last year.
frame_summary: The article argues that deniable, state-linked sabotage of defence-adjacent manufacturers sits awkwardly across property, business interruption, terrorism and war wordings, and that the government-backed terrorism pool does not reach it, so brokers should establish which policy responds before an incident rather than during a claim.
verbatim_quote: but its cover typically applies to certified acts of terrorism rather than the broader, greyer category of state-linked sabotage or acts of war - a distinction that matters enormously when a claim is being assessed.
verbatim_list: The threat lands only days after it emerged that hackers linked to Iran's regime managed to knock a UK power generation facility offline for four days last month - reportedly the first time a state-linked cyber intrusion has succeeded in forcing a British electricity-generating site to shut down.
noting insurers paid out close to £200 million in UK cyber claims last year alone.

title: Political violence reinsurance tightens at 1 July renewal
key_claim: Howden Re's 1 July 2026 renewal analysis: global political violence and terrorism premium income is around US$1.5 billion against insured loss estimates approaching double that; many reinsurers are declining risks tied to Western interests and critical infrastructure such as airports, refineries, desalination plants and ports; new MGAs and syndicates are entering the class and the Fidelis Partnership launched a consortium with up to US$47.5 million per risk in the Middle East.
frame_summary: The article argues that the political violence and terrorism class is repricing and retreating from critical infrastructure and Western-linked risks after the Middle East strikes, even as new capacity arrives in small lines, and that this tightening stands apart from a broadly softening July property renewal.
verbatim_quote: Global premium income for the class is estimated at around US$1.5 billion, against insured loss estimates already approaching double that figure.
verbatim_list: Many are declining risks tied to Western interests and critical infrastructure such as airports, refineries, desalination plants, and ports.
New capacity is entering the market from recently established MGAs and syndicates setting up PV&T as a line of business.
Early estimates suggest insured losses from the recent strikes could exceed US$3 billion, with total economic and uninsured losses expected to be materially higher.
Rates are rising alongside tighter underwriting controls, reduced line sizes, and higher attachment points, particularly for standalone political violence placements.

title: EIOPA insurance risk dashboard shows broadly stable risk environment even as cyber and geopolitical risk intensify
key_claim: EIOPA's July 2026 Insurance Risk Dashboard, built on Solvency II data from 96 groups and 2,091 solo undertakings, assesses insurance risks at medium despite deterioration in loss ratios and uncertainty around war- and trade-related coverages, and raises digitalisation and cyber risks to high, citing geopolitical tensions and elevated cyber underwriting exposures.
frame_summary: EIOPA is arguing that the European insurance sector is stable in aggregate but that the uncertainty is concentrated in war-related coverage terms and cyber exposures, which is where geopolitical tension reaches insurers' balance sheets.

title: Terrorism risk continues to evolve amid global instability, yet insurance market remains resilient (Global Terrorism Risk Insurance Report 2026)
key_claim: Marsh's Global Terrorism Risk Insurance Report 2026 finds terrorism threats have shifted to dispersed networks using cyberattacks and political violence; (re)insurers can offer per-risk terrorism capacity of $1 billion to $4 billion against roughly $1.2 trillion of total US sector capital; and the market's stability in the US rests on TRIPRA, the federal backstop, which is set to expire at the end of 2027.
frame_summary: Marsh is arguing that the terrorism insurance market is stable only because public-private backstops such as TRIPRA anchor the systemic tail, and that reauthorisation before the end-2027 expiry is what keeps that stability in place as threats blur into political violence and cyber.
verbatim_quote: Central to this stability in the US is the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program Reauthorization Act (TRIPRA), which provides a vital federal backstop and is set to expire at the end of 2027.
